title: Tooth Anatomy Guide: 32 Permanent & 20 Primary | Corpus
description: Master tooth anatomy with interactive charts for all 32 permanent and 20 primary teeth, Universal and FDI numbering, enamel, dentin, pulp, and tooth nerve.
h1: Tooth Anatomy and Dental Chart: 32 Permanent and 20 Primary Teeth
blurb: Interactive Universal (#1–32 / A–T) and FDI two-digit dental charts, four tooth classes, enamel-dentin-pulp layers, periodontal ligaments, and V2/V3 nerves.
lead: Every human tooth is a living organ anchored in jawbone by a shock-absorbing periodontal ligament, crowned with the hardest mineralized tissue in the body: dental enamel. In this illustrated guide to tooth anatomy and dental chart, we examine 76 documented structures—including anatomical crown, enamel, dentin, pulp chamber—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Every human tooth is a living organ anchored in jawbone by a shock-absorbing periodontal ligament, crowned with the hardest mineralized tissue in the body: dental enamel. Dental anatomy links each named tooth position to a tooth class and a representative cross-section. The crown bears enamel over dentin; roots bear cementum and anchor in the jaw through the periodontal ligament. Pulp contains nerves and vessels that communicate through root canals and apical foramina. Incisors cut, canines grip, premolars crush, and molars grind, although roots and cusps vary. A full permanent arch has 32 positions including third molars; primary dentition has 20, without premolars. This chart uses Universal and FDI numbering while explicitly distinguishing patient right from viewer left. Upper dental sensation primarily follows maxillary CN V2 superior alveolar branches, and lower dental sensation mandibular CN V3 inferior alveolar branches; facial nerve CN VII moves expression muscles but does not supply pulp sensation. Within the human body, the teeth · dental anatomy (Dentes permanentes et decidui) is situated in alveolar sockets of upper maxillae and lower mandible, within the oral cavity, receives arterial perfusion via superior and inferior alveolar arterial branches serve tooth pulps and supporting tissues, and is innervated by CN V2 superior alveolar branches: upper teeth; CN V3 inferior alveolar branches: lower teeth.

Structurally, the anatomical crown (Corona dentis) comprises part of the tooth covered by enamel, even if gingiva later covers a small portion. The clinical crown is the portion exposed in the mouth. Physiologically, the anatomical crown governs offers a cutting or grinding surface depending on tooth class. Structurally, the enamel (Enamelum) comprises highly mineralized outer cover of the crown, shown white above the gum; enamel does not normally cover the root. Physiologically, the enamel protects deeper dentin from wear and acid, though it can demineralize. Structurally, the dentin (Dentinum) comprises yellowish tissue beneath crown enamel and root cementum; surrounds pulp throughout the tooth. Physiologically, the dentin supports the crown and houses dentinal tubules. The pulp chamber (Cavitas pulpae) is central space in the crown holding vascular, neural and connective dental pulp; its roof lies under occlusal dentin. Physiologically, the pulp chamber supports tooth vitality, defense and dentin formation. Structurally, the tooth root (Radix dentis) comprises portion anchored below the crown in an alveolar socket; molar roots may be multiple but number and canal shape vary. Physiologically, the tooth root anchors the tooth through periodontal ligament and cementum. The root canal (Canalis radicis dentis) is narrow continuation of the pulp space inside each root, opening toward its apex. Physiologically, the root canal governs conveys pulpal nerve and blood supply through the root.

Clinically, regarding the anatomical crown, do not confuse anatomical crown with clinical crown. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the enamel, once mature enamel is lost, it does not regrow as an intact enamel layer. In clinical pathology involving the dentin, exposed dentin can be sensitive and is more vulnerable than enamel. Medical evaluation of the pulp chamber also notes that deep caries can inflame pulp; a digital cutaway cannot diagnose pulp disease.

questions.question: What are the main layers of a tooth crown and root?
questions.answer: Crown dentin is covered by enamel; root dentin is covered by cementum. Pulp occupies the central chamber and canals, while the periodontal ligament connects the root to its alveolar socket. These are distinct tissues, not interchangeable layers.

questions.question: Which nerves carry sensation from upper and lower teeth?
questions.answer: Upper teeth receive sensation mainly through superior alveolar branches of CN V2; lower teeth receive it through the inferior alveolar branch of CN V3.

questions.question: How are permanent and primary teeth numbered?
questions.answer: The Universal system labels 32 conventional permanent positions 1–32 and 20 primary positions A–T. The two-digit FDI system uses quadrants 1–4 for permanent teeth and 5–8 for primary teeth, with a second digit for position within each quadrant.

questions.question: Do adults always have 32 teeth and do primary teeth have premolars?
questions.answer: The full permanent dentition usually has 32 teeth, including third molars, but some adults have fewer because third molars may be absent or removed. Primary dentition has 20 teeth and no premolars.

questions.question: Can one molar cutaway show the exact canal and root shape of every tooth?
questions.answer: No. Root, canal and cusp anatomy vary by tooth class and individual. This is a representative teaching model, not a patient scan or a rendering of every tooth.
